_meta.comment: Per-plan usage limits and the assumptions behind the 'break even at' and 'ceiling' columns on pricing.html. Joins to extension/prices.json 'subscriptions' on p + m (exact string match). Rates are NOT stored here — they are read live from prices.json.api at render time, so these figures re-price themselves when API prices change.

provenance_legend.disclosed: The provider publishes this figure about its own product.
provenance_legend.derived: Computed from a disclosed absolute cap and a disclosed multiplier, both from the provider.
provenance_legend.third_party: Measured or reported by someone other than the provider. Treat as indicative.
provenance_legend.not_disclosed: The provider does not publish a usable figure.

_meta.finding: As of August 2026, exactly one absolute consumer usage figure is published by any major provider about its own product, and it is a feature sub-limit rather than a general allowance: 'Go users can send up to 10 messages every 5 hours after enabling Thinking.' Nothing else is quantified anywhere. Every tier is sold on a relative multiplier against a base nobody quantifies: OpenAI's Pro tiers as '5x or 20x more usage' than Plus (what it multiplies is unstated), Anthropic's Max as '5x/20x more usage than Pro', Google's tiers as '2x/4x/20x higher than standard limits' — Google's own footnote clarifying the base as 'non-AI subscribers'. Anthropic, Google and OpenAI have all moved to metering that varies with prompt complexity, feature use, model and chat length. Google reserves the right to change limits 'without notice, including due to capacity constraints.' The pattern is consistent: disclosure gets worse as the price goes up.
_meta.context_windows_are_now_disclosed: Counter-example to the finding above, added 2026-08-24, and recorded because a file that only collects evidence for its own thesis is not evidence. OpenAI's plan table now publishes a per-plan CONTEXT WINDOW for every consumer tier — Instant 27K/54K/54K/128K and Reasoning Varies/256K/256K/400K across Free/Go/Plus/Pro. That is a real, absolute, provider-published number about its own product, and the first any provider has ADDED rather than withdrawn in the period this file covers. It does not weaken the finding, because a context window bounds how much fits in one conversation, not how many conversations you get — the allowance question is still unanswered everywhere. But "nobody discloses anything" would now be false, and the honest statement is narrower: nobody discloses an ALLOWANCE.
_meta.disclosure_is_getting_worse: Between the 2026-07-28 and 2026-08-08 checks, OpenAI DELETED the only general absolute cap anyone published — '160 GPT-5.5 Instant messages per 3 hours', which had applied identically to Go at $8 and Plus at $20. The replacement language is that limits 'can be dynamic and may vary based on factors that include market, system conditions, abuse-prevention guardrails, and individual usage'. ChatGPT Plus is now the most expensive consumer tier of any provider carrying no published usage figure of any kind. This is worth re-checking every time this file is verified: the trend is one-directional, and a figure being here today is not evidence it will be next quarter.

archetypes.comment: Tokens per message exchange. DERIVED, not hand-picked: scripts/derive-archetypes.js measures characters-per-token with the real cl100k tokenizer over this repo’s prose (3.882 chars/token, 165 samples) and converts the message lengths below. Read that honestly: the CONVERSION is measured, the LENGTHS are still an assumption — prompt_chars, reply_chars and history_turns are judgement, chosen to be checkable against a real chat window rather than legible as round token counts. “input” is this prompt plus history_turns prior exchanges re-sent; “output” is the reply, BEFORE the reasoning multiplier in _meta.reasoning is applied. This is still the largest single lever on every figure on the page. There is no corpus of real chat traffic here, so do not call these measurements; the intended anchor remains real EcoMeter exports. check-auditor.js re-runs the derivation and fails if this block has drifted from it.

reasoning.comment: Thinking-token multipliers on the OUTPUT side. A reasoning model emits hidden chain-of-thought before its visible reply and bills it at the output rate, so a break-even that counts only the reply understates what the same work costs on the API — which pushes the break-even figure UP and makes a plan look harder to justify than it is. EcoMeter has modelled this since it shipped (REASONING_RANGES in extension/sidepanel.js); the website did not, and the gap was worth 30-45% on exactly the frontier models people pay for. mid is applied; lo/hi record the spread rather than pretending there is not one. THESE ARE ESTIMATES, and coarse ones: providers publish no per-model thinking-token statistics at all, so nobody outside them can measure it. Applies to the models that reason BY DEFAULT in consumer chat, which is why gpt-5.6-luna and the flash/mini tiers are absent rather than set to 1.
reasoning.basis: Ranges follow the shape EcoMeter already used for the o-series and R1 (1-10x depending on task complexity, mid nearer the low end because ordinary chat is not the hard case). Extended to the current default-thinking frontier models on 2026-08-26. Unverifiable against provider data; revise on any published figure.

throughput.basis: One message exchange per minute of active use — time to read the reply and write the next prompt. A round number, chosen to be legible rather than precise; it is an assumption, not a measurement.
throughput.waking_hours_basis: Used only to flag caps that cannot be reached by a person in a day.

caveats: Break-even is what the same usage would cost at the provider's own published API rates. The API is not the product: no app, no memory, no file handling, no support. Treat it as a floor on value, not a full accounting.

The tokens-per-message archetypes are HALF assumption and half measurement, and the halves must not be confused. Message lengths (prompt_chars, reply_chars, history_turns) are judgement; the characters-to-tokens conversion is measured with the real cl100k tokenizer by scripts/derive-archetypes.js, which owns the numbers. Still the single largest lever on every figure here. Lengths stated in characters rather than tokens on purpose: a person can check '1,800-character reply' against a real chat window, and cannot check '500 output tokens'.

Thinking tokens ARE now priced, at _meta.reasoning mid, for the models that reason by default. A reasoning model emits hidden chain-of-thought before its reply and bills it at the output rate, so counting only the visible reply understated API cost by 30-45% on exactly the frontier models people pay for. The multipliers are estimates and coarse ones — no provider publishes per-model thinking-token statistics, so this cannot be verified from outside. It is modelled anyway, unlike search fees and caching, because the omission was one-directional and large, and because EcoMeter has modelled it since it shipped: leaving the site out of step with our own extension was the harder position to defend.
Ceiling figures assume the cap is hit in every window, every day, for 30 days. Essentially nobody does this. It is an upper bound, not an expectation.
Prompt caching is not modelled, consistent with EcoMeter. Cached input bills far less, so real API cost is lower than shown and break-even is correspondingly harder to reach.
Where a cap is a soft fallback rather than a hard stop (OpenAI downgrades to mini rather than cutting you off), the ceiling understates total value and overstates top-model value.

Every Gemini break-even is currently computed on gemini-3.6-flash, whose API rate is PROMOTIONAL until 2026-12-31 (half the standard rate). These figures will roughly halve in the number of messages they name when that promo ends — they re-price themselves from prices.json, so no edit is needed here, but a Gemini plan looks better value today than it will in January. check-prices.js fails on the promo date.

xAI publishes ONE model row on its plan comparison — Grok 4.6 — so every SuperGrok tier gets a single break-even figure rather than a range. We previously paired it with grok-4.3, which x.ai does not offer on any consumer plan.

Perplexity break-even is deliberately priced on THIRD-PARTY models, using the provider:model form (e.g. anthropic:claude-opus-5). Perplexity’s help centre publishes a per-plan model table and it is almost all frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and xAI: Pro serves GPT-5.6 Terra, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 5 and Grok 4.5; Max adds GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5. Sonar is excluded from the calculation on purpose, for two reasons: the app model is now branded Sonar 2 and carries no published API rate under that name, and the Sonar API adds a per-request search fee ($5 per 1,000 requests) on top of tokens that this cost model does not carry — pricing it at token rates alone understates API cost, which pushes break-even UP and makes the plan look harder to justify than it is. (An earlier version of this note had that backwards.) Perplexity also states the Sonar chat API is superseded by the Agent API and supported only until 2026-09-27.

NO BREAK-EVEN HERE CARRIES THE COST OF SEARCH, AND EVERY PROVIDER BUT ONE CHARGES FOR IT. Surveyed 2026-08-26 on provider-owned pages: OpenAI web search $10 per 1,000 calls ($25 on the non-reasoning preview tool); Anthropic web search $10 per 1,000 searches; Google grounding with Google Search 5,000 free per month across Gemini 3.x then $14 per 1,000 requests; xAI web_search and x_search $5 per 1,000 calls each; Perplexity $5 per 1,000 requests on the Sonar models; Mistral states tool APIs are priced per call without publishing the figure. DeepSeek is the only one with no per-request fee at all. Our cost per message is tokens only, so for anyone whose chat routinely searches the web, real API cost is higher than we model and break-even is therefore LOWER than we print — the plan is easier to justify than these numbers say. We do not model it because we have no honest figure for how often a given person’s messages trigger a search, and inventing one would be worse than the gap. Same treatment as prompt caching, which biases the other way.
Microsoft plans have no break-even figure: Copilot runs on OpenAI models but Microsoft publishes no equivalent per-token rate to compare against.

plans.stated: The plans page advertises 'Unlimited text chats with GPT-5.6 Luna' — 'subject to abuse guardrails' — alongside limited messages, uploads, image generation and voice. So the headline is unlimited-on-the-cheapest-model rather than a capped allowance on the default one. GPT-5.5 has now FINISHED leaving this tier: it sits in the plan table's single 'Legacy models' row, marked No for Free and No for Go, and the Free Tier FAQ updated 2026-08-13 lists only Luna. On 2026-08-08 that rollout was still in progress and 5.5 was correctly recorded as present then. No absolute message figure either way. Free gets no GPT-5.6 Sol at any reasoning level; its Think button runs Thinking Mini.
plans.source: https://openai.com/chatgpt/pricing + help.openai.com ChatGPT Free Tier FAQ

caps.note: Enabled via + then Thinking. Explicitly does NOT use GPT-5.6 Sol. scope_limited: this bounds ONE FEATURE, not the plan — ordinary Go chat is advertised as unlimited on Luna, so a ceiling computed from this figure would sit far below what Go is actually worth. Consumers must refuse it the same way they refuse an undisclosed multiplier base.

plans.stated: The only absolute MESSAGE figure OpenAI still publishes for a consumer tier: 'Go users can send up to 10 messages every 5 hours after enabling Thinking.' Everything else is 'more messages' than Free. Go carries ads ('This plan may include ads'), and as of 2026-08-24 GPT-5.5 has left this tier along with Free — the 'Legacy models' row reads No for Go.
plans.note: REMOVED 2026-08-08: a '160 GPT-5.5 Instant messages / 3h' cap, previously recorded here as disclosed for both Go and Plus. OpenAI's help article no longer states any absolute Instant figure — it now says only that limits 'can be dynamic and may vary based on factors that include market, system conditions, abuse-prevention guardrails, and individual usage'. It was the single disclosed absolute this whole file rested on, and it is gone.

plans.stated: 'Expanded messages and uploads' over Go, and 'Limits apply'. No absolute MESSAGE figure. The '160 GPT-5.5 Instant messages / 3h' cap recorded here until 2026-08-08 is no longer published — see the note on ChatGPT Go. Plus remains the most expensive consumer tier of any provider publishing no usage allowance of any kind. It does now publish a context window (54K Instant / 256K Reasoning) — a real disclosure, but a per-conversation size limit, not an allowance.
plans.note: Plus includes GPT-5.6 Sol at Medium and High reasoning but not Extra High or Pro, which are Pro-only. Free and Go get no Sol access at all, at any reasoning level. If a Sol reasoning limit is reached, ChatGPT falls back to GPT-5.4 Thinking mini rather than stopping.

plans.stated: 'Pro $100 unlocks 5x higher usage than Plus.' What it multiplies is not stated: the one published absolute cap (160 GPT-5.5 Instant messages / 3h) is identical on Go at $8 and Plus at $20, so it is plainly not the figure that separates tiers. OpenAI adds only that 'some models have separate usage allowances' — those allowances are never published.

'Pro $200 unlocks 20x usage than Plus.' What it multiplies is not stated — see the $100 tier. Multiplying the published Instant cap by 20 would imply 25,600 messages a day, which is not a claim OpenAI makes and not one worth repeating.
'Free for everyone.' No usage figure published.

'More usage' than Free. Anthropic describes a 'conversation budget' that varies with 'length and complexity of your conversations, the features you use, which Claude model you're chatting with, and the effort level you've selected', and publishes no numbers.

third_party.why: The strongest third-party figure on this page. Several independent trackers converge on ~45 per 5 hours, and it is internally consistent with the separately-reported ~225 per 5 hours on Max 5x (exactly 5x). Still an estimate: Anthropic publishes nothing, the 5-hour caps were doubled on 2026-05-06 so older figures are stale, and Anthropic says the real budget varies with conversation length, features, model and effort level.

plans.note: A weekly cap sits under the 5-hour window and binds first, so the limit cannot be hit every day for 30 days.

plans.stated: '5x more usage than Pro' — a disclosed multiplier against an undisclosed base.
'20x more usage than Pro' — a disclosed multiplier against an undisclosed base.
'Standard limits' — never quantified. Compute-based, refreshing every 5 hours up to a weekly limit.
'2x higher than standard limits' — a disclosed multiplier against an undisclosed base.
'4x higher than standard limits' — a disclosed multiplier against an undisclosed base.
'5x higher than AI Pro limits.' Pay-as-you-go credits can be bought to continue past the limit.
'20x higher than AI Pro limits.' Pay-as-you-go credits can be bought to continue past the limit.

plans._comment: x.ai/pricing ticks Grok 4.6 in EVERY column, Free included, so every xAI tier is valued on the same pair: what you buy is rate limit, never model access. The previous entries valued these tiers on grok-3 / grok-3-mini / grok-4, all of which had already left xAI's pricing page — the free tier was being valued on a two-generation-old model.
New tier between SuperGrok and Heavy, found on x.ai/pricing 2026-08-24. xAI publishes no usage figure for it — the card says 'significantly higher usage' against a base it never quantifies.

third_party.why: Sources disagree — some report 3 per day as of July 2026 rather than 5. Perplexity publishes no figure, so there is no way to settle it.

plans.stated: Pro Search is marketed as unlimited. Perplexity does not publish the limit that actually binds — the weekly allowance on advanced models — and has confirmed it is not even the same for every Pro subscriber.

third_party.why: Midpoint of the 100-150 per week that Pro users reported in May 2026 after limits were cut; standard Pro Search was unaffected. Weak for an unusual reason: Perplexity's own response was that 'some users are seeing different usage limits because their accounts are tied to promotional-code offers, and we've had to adjust enforcement due to fraud and unauthorized resale' — i.e. the provider confirms the limit differs between subscribers on the same plan. There may be no single true number to find.
third_party.replaces: An earlier 600 searches/day figure, dropped: it described unlimited Pro Search rather than the advanced-model allowance that actually binds.

plans.stated: Marketed as unlimited Pro searches with no daily or hourly cap; no figure published and 'unlimited' is not a number we can price.

'Extensive use' beyond the standard credit limit. Microsoft publishes a hard 60 AI credits/month for the cheaper Personal and Family plans but no figure for Premium — disclosure decreasing as price rises.
'Limited messages and web searches' — no number.

third_party.why: Single source, described as a soft cap. Mistral's own help-centre articles on Le Chat limits now 404, so there is nothing to check it against.

plans.stated: Messages are 'subject to fair usage limits and Mistral's Terms of Service' — unquantified. Mistral does publish one number on its pricing page: 150 Flash answers per day on Pro (200 on Team). Flash answers are one feature, not the general message allowance.

third_party.why: Treat with real suspicion. The widely-repeated '150 messages/day soft cap' for Le Chat Pro is the same number Mistral publishes for Flash answers per day — a specific feature, not a general message limit. Most likely one figure misread as the other. Kept because it is the only general-message estimate in circulation, but the coincidence is not reassuring.

plans.stated: No paid consumer tier and no published chat usage limits.
